newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan denies rebel claim of Maban fall.
newsitem.headline: Sudan denies rebel claim of Maban fall.

text.p: Sudan on Friday denied the fall of Maban into rebel hands on the southern front of the Blue Nile region, an area where a Swiss-based relief group said Sudanese troops were bombing and burning to drive out the rebels.
Sudanese rebels in Asmara and Cairo said a joint rebel force had captured the town, which they say is a strategic bypass for the White Nile state, Upper Nile and the Blue Nile region.
In Cairo, the opposition National Democratic Alliance (NDA) called on the army to revolt and promised Khartoum's Islamist government more defeats.

Sudanese Information Minister and government spokesman Brigadier al-Tayeb Ibrahim Mohamed Khair denied the rebel claim, telling a news briefing in Khartoum that the situation in the Blue Nile area "is quiet with no movement on the enemy side".

The Sudanese government-owned al-Ingaz al-Watani newspaper quoted Khair as saying Sudanese forces had killed 63 Eritrean soldiers and seized a large amount of arms in the eastern state of Kassala. He did not say when.
Sudan says neighbouring Eritrea and Ethiopia are orchestrating the fighting but both countries, which host Sudanese rebels, reject the allegations.

Ethiopia has written to the U.N. Security Council denying charges by Khartoum that Addis Ababa was involved in the fighting. Sudan has already asked the Security Council to debate the latest fighting in the south.

Northern and southern rebels working together in their first combined offensive to overthrow Khartoum's Islamist government say they are responsible for the attacks against army units in the east, which began earlier this week.
The rebels say their objective is not to capture Khartoum but to strangle it and provoke an uprising against President Omar Hassan al-Bashir's Islamist military government.

Yassir Arman, spokesman for John Garang, head of the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) and chairman of a joint military command, told Reuters in Asmara 980 members of the government army militia had surrendered after the fall of Maban to the rebels, who were now marching towards Damazin.
Damazin is about 480 km (300 miles) southeast of Khartoum and supplies Khartoum with up to 80 percent of its power.
The rebels say they have already seized two towns on the border with Ethiopia -- Kurmuk and Qeissan.
"The regime in Khartoum must know that it has only a minority following and that victory in the end will be for the Sudanese people," said opposition spokesman in Cairo Farouk Abu Issa.
"That 980 people surrendered shows that the regime's grip on its own people is weak. We call on the army to join our coalition to cleanse Sudan of this regime," he told Reuters.
The Swiss-based Christian Solidarity International (CSI) said on Friday Sudan had launched a "scorched earth" policy in which had left some 50,000 people on the verge of starvation.
CSI said a two-member team it sent on a covert visit last week to the south of the Blue Nile region reported government forces were "bombing and torching" villages across the area.

"The government of Sudan is waging a new scorched earth policy against its own civilians in the closed areas of east-central Sudan near the Ethiopian border," said a statement from CSI, which has its headquarters in Zurich.

President Omar Hassan al-Bashir, in a television broadcast on Thursday, vowed to stand strong against the attacks while convoys of government soldiers, members of the paramilitary Popular Defence Forces and volunteers headed for Kassala and the southeastern Blue Nile state.

"What is going on in the eastern front is a Zionist, imperialist plot being implemented by Eritrea and Ethiopia aimed at setting up a secular, African state in Sudan instead of the present state," said Bashir, a lieutenant-general who seized power in a coup in 1989.
"Sudan will face off any attack as a duty to our religion and nation," Bashir said. He said he did not rule out an attack on the entire length of Sudan's eastern front.
